rationale: A wins because it gives the founder four clean reporter doors, especially "Your health plan may now include Calm Premium at no cost. Here is how to check." B has usable bones, but its first swing, "Calm goes from $70-a-year subscription to a covered insurance benefit," invents a price in the headline. That is not seasoning; that is a fact-checking problem wearing a hat.
gaps_in_A: "pointing to a randomized trial as the reason" asserts payer motivation the update does not give. The insurers may have used the study, but the facts only say Calm is publishing one.

"the insurer partnership and the study land together" and "same-day timing" overstate chronology. The update packages the deal and study together; it does not prove the insurers signed after seeing the paper or that both were announced the same day.
"Next step: `journalist-fit-check`" is slightly early. Before outreach, Calm needs the insurer names, journal link, payment structure, and study-method basics nailed down.
gaps_in_B: "$70-a-year subscription" is invented. The update says Calm Premium is free to covered members and that Calm has 4M+ paid subscribers; it gives no subscription price.
"consumer subscription apps survive once growth slows" sneaks in a growth-slowdown narrative with no support. A business reporter will ask for churn, growth, or retention data immediately.

"Wellness apps are crossing from app-store impulse buy into reimbursed health benefit" overclaims a trend from one Calm deal, then admits it needs "comparable recent examples." That should be framed as conditional, not sold as a trend angle yet.

B leaves the 25M-member service story on the floor. No angle makes the covered member the protagonist, even though "members of three national insurers get Calm Premium at no cost" is the cleanest consumer-service hook.
